_note: Plain-English explanations for the jargon on this site. Written by hand, not generated: a model that invented definitions would be the one thing here you could not check. Built and checked by tools/gen_glossary.py, which refuses any explanation that runs long or leans on more jargon. Each entry carries the domain and shape tags Cypha uses as its feature vector — see assets/js/glossary.js.

terms.g: The boss program inside a computer. Everything else has to ask it before it can touch the screen, the disk or the network.
The software a computer runs before any of your programs. Windows, macOS and Linux are operating systems. It hands out the machine to everything else.
How a normal program asks the boss program for something it cannot do itself, like open a file or send a message.
Everything on a computer that is not the boss program. Your browser, your editor, your games. It has to ask for everything.
One program while it is actually running. Your computer keeps them apart so a crash in one does not take the others down.
One line of work inside a program. A program with several threads can do several things at once.
The computer's short-term workspace. Fast, and wiped when the power goes off. Programs keep what they are working on here.
The filing cabinet. It is what turns a disk full of ones and zeros into folders and files with names.
Starting a computer up from cold. A bootable disk is one a machine can actually start from.
Software baked into a device, running before anything else. It is the first thing that wakes up when you press the button.
Code that runs with nothing underneath it, so none of the usual help is there. The boss program has to be written this way.
The handshake rules two lumps of finished code follow so they can call each other. Break the rules and they stop fitting together.
The list of things one program will let another ask it to do. A menu, basically.
The part you click on. Windows, buttons, menus. The opposite of typing commands.
Driving a computer by typing instructions instead of clicking. Uglier, much faster once you know it.
A version of the FreeBSD operating system with extra defences built in. ParanoidBSD starts from it instead of starting from nothing.
A free operating system anyone can read and change. A cousin of the one inside a Mac. Common in network gear and servers.
A family of free operating systems that share the same ancestor. FreeBSD and HardenedBSD are both in it.
The free operating system that runs most of the internet. Same job as Windows, given away and open to read.
A desktop you can look at and click on, for Linux and BSD. Windows, taskbar, settings, the lot.
A toolkit for building windows and buttons that work the same on Windows, Mac and Linux. Used here for the desktop programs.
A computer whose job is answering other computers. Nobody sits in front of it.
Moving software so it runs somewhere it did not before. Rewriting the bits that were tied to the old place.
One self-contained piece of a program, with a clear edge. You can work on it without holding the whole thing in your head.
A line of steps where each one hands its result to the next, like a factory belt.
The text a person actually writes. It is the recipe; the program is the meal.
A translator that turns the text a person wrote into the numbers a machine can run. To compile is to run it through.
The finished program, as the machine holds it: numbers, not words. Unreadable to a person without help.
A programming language used where speed and control matter. The 23 is the 2023 edition of its rules.
An old, fast, bare-bones programming language. Almost every operating system is still built on it, which is much of the problem.
A newer programming language that refuses to compile most memory mistakes. Fast like C, far harder to get wrong.
A programming language that reads almost like English. Slower to run, much quicker to write.
The machinery a lot of translators are built on. Clang is the one that handles C and C++.
A halfway form, between the text a person wrote and the numbers a machine runs. Comparing two of them shows whether two programs really do the same thing.
A way to run fast, compiled programs inside a web page. It is why the demos on this site work without installing anything.
The folder where a project lives, with every past version of every file kept. Usually shared online.
One saved change to a project, with a note about what it was and who did it. The history is a list of these.
Taking your own copy of somebody's project and going your own way with it. Forkable means nothing stops you.
The website where most open projects keep their files and their history. Free to read without an account.
The front page of a project's folder. What it is, what it does, and what it does not do.
Software whose recipe is public, so anyone can read it, check it and build it. Not the same as free of charge.
A small program whose only job is checking that another program still does what it should. Run them every time you change something.
The tool that runs all the checks for a project and reports which ones failed.
A robot that rebuilds the project and runs every check each time somebody changes a file. It catches breakage the same day.
A rule that stops a change getting in until the checks pass. No argument, no exceptions.
A fixed test everyone runs, so two different things can be compared on the same ground. Doing well on your own test proves nothing.
A check that something which used to work still works. Named after the thing it stops: quietly going backwards.
Run the old version and the new version on the same input and compare. If they ever disagree, the new one is wrong.
A known-correct answer saved on purpose, so later runs can be checked against it.
A written record of where each piece came from. It is how you can still tell, years later, who wrote what and under what rules.
A placeholder that has the right shape but does nothing yet. It lets the rest of the work carry on around the hole.
Tidying code without changing what it does. A rewrite pass is a tool that does one kind of tidying, everywhere, by itself.
Making sure a program only touches the memory it was handed. Get it wrong and you have a hole. Roughly two in three serious holes are this one mistake.
A program keeps using a locker after handing the key back. Someone else gets that locker, and now they can read or change what the program is doing.
Pouring more data in than the space set aside for it, so the rest spills into whatever sat next door. A classic way to take over a program.
A key that opens one door and nothing else. Give a program that key and it can only do that one thing.
The small core of the system that hands out those keys, and turns away every request that does not carry one.
A ticket that stands for one thing a program is allowed to use. No ticket, no access.
When a program can do anything you can do, just because it is running as you. It is why one hacked app can read every file you own.
A FreeBSD feature that lets a program lock itself down, so from then on it can only use what it already holds.
A box a program is run inside, so if it goes bad it cannot reach anything outside the box.
A rule that memory can be written to, or run as code, but never both. It stops an attacker writing new instructions and then running them.
Shuffling where things sit in memory every time a program starts, so an attacker cannot know in advance where to aim.
A defence that does not fix the bug but makes it much harder to use. Locks on the windows, not a new wall.
A watchdog built into the program while testing. It shouts the moment the program touches memory it should not, instead of quietly carrying on.
Throwing millions of random, malformed inputs at a program to see what makes it fall over. Crude, and it finds real bugs.
A piece of work that turns a bug into actual control of the machine. Knowing the bug is not the same as having one.
Someone from outside going through the work line by line, looking for what the author missed. Unaudited means nobody has yet.
Writing down exactly who you are defending against and what they can do. Without one, secure means nothing.
Scrambling a message so only the person with the right key can read it. Everyone else sees noise.
Encryption that also proves nobody tampered with the message. You learn it was changed instead of reading something false.
A number used once and never again, to stop two scrambled messages coming out looking the same. Reuse one and the whole thing can unravel.
The scrambling method almost everything uses, from your bank to your phone. Decades old and still unbroken.
A fixed-length fingerprint of any piece of data. Same data, same fingerprint. Change one letter and the fingerprint changes completely.
A simple either-or rule: true when one side is true, but not when both are. Half of all secret codes lean on it.
Arithmetic with only two numbers, 0 and 1, where adding is the either-or rule. Exactly how a chip already works.
Learning a secret from something other than the message: how long it took, how much power it drew, how loud the fan got.
Everything about a message except what it says: who, when, how big, how often. Usually more revealing than the message.
Working out who is talking to whom by watching the shape of the traffic, without reading a word of it.
A relay chain that shuffles messages and sends them on, so nobody watching can match what went in to what came out.
A message format for relay chains where each hop peels off one layer and learns nothing but the next hop.
Sending at the same steady rate whether you have anything to say or not, padding with nothing. A watcher cannot tell talking from silence.
Someone who can watch every wire everywhere but never touch anything. The hardest opponent to hide from, and the one to design against.
Fake messages sent to keep the real ones company, so the real ones do not stand out.
The wait between asking and getting an answer. Privacy usually costs latency; there is no way round it.
How much data can go down the pipe per second. Not the same as how long it takes to start arriving.
The ordinary internet, outside any privacy network. Leaving into it is the weakest point of any such system.
Matching what went in against what came out by timing alone. If the pattern lines up, the link is exposed.
Being lost in a crowd. The bigger the crowd behaving the same way, the better hidden you are.
A tool that reads a finished program and tries to work backwards to readable text. Like guessing the recipe from the cake.
Something shaped like code that a person can follow, but that nobody could run. Most decompilers stop here.
Working out how something does what it does without being told. Usually because nobody kept the recipe.
The lowest readable form of a program: one tiny machine instruction per line. True, and almost impossible to read in bulk.
The file shape a finished program takes on Linux and BSD. Windows uses a different one.
The file shape a finished program takes on Windows. Every .exe is one.
Flattening something out so it can be saved or sent, and put back together at the other end.
Several things happening in a program at once. It is where the hardest bugs live, because the order changes every run.
The human-readable names left inside a program. Strip them and the work gets far harder. Name-blind means working with none.
Software that gets better at a job by being shown examples, instead of being told the rules step by step.
The thing that comes out of showing a program lots of examples. A big pile of numbers that turns a question into an answer.
Showing a program examples over and over and nudging its numbers each time it gets one wrong.
The numbers inside a model. They are all it knows. Training is just the slow business of changing them.
Another word for those numbers. More of them means more room to learn, and more to get wrong.
Layers of simple sums stacked up, each feeding the next. Nothing in there thinks; the stack as a whole does something useful.
The design behind almost every modern AI that handles language. Its trick is letting every word look at every other word.
Letting every word in a sentence check every other word before deciding what it means. Powerful, and the cost grows fast as the text gets longer.
A chunk of text an AI handles at one go, usually a word or part of one. Costs are counted in these.
Something that sorts each input into one of a fixed set of buckets. Spam or not spam.
Predicting a number rather than a bucket. How much, not which one.
A model that keeps learning while it is being used, from each new thing it sees, instead of being trained once and frozen.
Training a small model to copy a big one's answers. You keep most of the skill in a fraction of the size.
Examples kept back on purpose and never shown during training, so the score at the end means something.
When a model memorises the practice questions instead of learning the subject. Perfect on those, useless on anything new.
The simplest thing that could work, measured first. If the clever method cannot beat it, the clever method is not worth it.
How surprised a language model is by real text. Lower is better. Roughly: how many words it was torn between at each step.
How many bits a model needs to store each character of text. Lower means it understood the text better.
The hidden summary a model builds of something before it does anything with it. Squeezing a picture down to what matters.
Turning a word or thing into a list of numbers, so that similar things end up with similar lists.
Actually using a trained model to get an answer. The part you pay for every time, as opposed to training, which you pay for once.
An older, openly published language model. Small by today's standards, which makes it a fair yardstick to measure against.
A trick that bends data into a shape where a straight line can separate it. Cheap, and it makes a simple method behave like a complicated one.
Deliberately forcing a model through a narrow pipe, so it has to throw away everything except what actually matters.
The idea that the best explanation is the one you can write down in the fewest words. Simpler beats fancier unless fancier earns it.
A maths-only description of the perfect learner, which needs infinite computing power. Useless to run, useful to aim at.
The idea that a thing acts in order to be less surprised by what happens next. Curiosity, written as a sum.
Two things spreading and reacting on a surface. It makes spots and stripes on its own, the way animal markings form.
Cells that fire together wire together. A learning rule borrowed from brains, where each connection changes on its own local evidence.
One run of a model from input to answer. Normally nothing learns during it; here, something does.
The working-out a model does before answering. You are charged for it even though you often never see it.
Letting the thing that did the work also be the judge of whether the work is right. It is never allowed here.
The AI built for this site, from first principles rather than from a copy of somebody else's design. It sorts, predicts and keeps learning as it goes.
A fixed recipe for getting something done: these steps, in this order, every time.
The maths of things that happen at random but at a steady average rate. How many buses arrive in an hour.
Maths for events that make more events likely straight after. One burglary on a street makes the next one more likely, for a while.
A way of finding clumps in scattered points, without being told how many clumps to look for. Anything not in a clump is left out as noise.
Turning a scatter of dots into a smooth heat map, so the busy areas show up as hills.
Working backwards from where crimes happened to where the person probably lives. Offenders avoid their own doorstep, and that gap is the clue.
The standard set of building blocks for number crunching. Almost all heavy maths software sits on top of them.
The standard library for solving big systems of equations. Old, careful, and everywhere.
Splitting a grid of numbers into two simpler ones, so equations can be solved quickly. A workhorse, not a party trick.
Breaking a grid of numbers into its main directions, strongest first. Keep the top few and you have squeezed the data with little loss.
Finding the directions a system leaves pointing the same way, and how much it stretches each one. It is how you find its natural shape.
An equation about how something changes over time. Solving it tells you where the thing ends up.
An equation about how something changes over time and space at once. Weather and heat spreading are both this.
Chopping a shape into thousands of small pieces so a hard physical question can be answered piece by piece.
Simulating how air or water flows, by computer, instead of building it and blowing air at it.
Software that does algebra in symbols rather than numbers. It gives you x squared, not 4.
Searching for the best setting of some dials, when trying every combination would take longer than you have.
Treating a set of possible beliefs as a curved surface, so you can measure how far apart two beliefs really are.
Taking a step towards a better answer in a direction that accounts for the shape of the problem, rather than blindly downhill.
One number balancing two worries: how often you were right, and how much you missed. 1.0 is perfect, 0 is hopeless.
The bell curve. Most things near the middle, fewer out at the edges.
A whole number that only divides by itself and one. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11. They are the building blocks of every other number.
Squashing something with many numbers down to fewer, at random. Surprisingly, how far apart things are mostly survives the squash.
Scoring a word by how often it appears here and how rare it is everywhere else. It is how a search finds what a page is really about.
Measuring how alike two lists of numbers are by the angle between them, not their size. Pointing the same way means saying the same thing.
A licence that lets anyone use and change the software. One condition: hand your version to others and you hand over your changes too.
You can read all the code. Whether you can use it for anything you like is a separate question, answered by the licence.
The written permission that says what you are allowed to do with something somebody else made.
The same software offered two ways: free with strings attached, or paid with the strings cut. You pick.
A licence that passes its own rules on. Use this freely, but whatever you build from it has to be as free as it was.
Saying who made it. Most free licences ask for nothing else.
Changing the rules a piece of software is handed out under. Only the person who wrote it can, which is why inherited code keeps its old rules.
A funding rule: hit the target and every pledge is taken, miss it and nobody is charged a cent.
Promising money to a campaign. Nothing leaves your account unless the campaign reaches its target.
Asking a lot of people for a small amount each, up front, to pay for something that does not exist yet.
Something a campaign gives back to the people who paid. Here there is exactly one, and everything else is a plain donation.
Australian dollars. Roughly two thirds of a US dollar, though that moves.
Raw computer time, bought by the hour or by the job. It is the one thing this project is asking money for.
Money that goes on running the thing rather than on the thing itself. Fees, postage, admin.
A program that plays chess by looking ahead through millions of positions and scoring each one.
How many moves ahead a program looks. Each extra move ahead costs many times more work than the one before.
A way of looking ahead that stops exploring a line as soon as it is clearly worse than one already found. Same answer, far less work.
A score for a chess position, in pawns. Plus two means you are about two pawns better off.
A rating for how strong a player is. Beat stronger players and it climbs; a 200-point gap means the stronger one wins about three games in four.
The first several moves of a chess game, worked out long ago and memorised rather than calculated.
The last stage of a chess game, with few pieces left. It is more about counting than about ideas.
The written statement of what something must do, agreed before it is built. Without one, done is just an opinion.
Proving the thing actually does what it was meant to, by checking, not by looking at it and feeling good.
Same input, same answer, every single time. No luck involved, so a failure can always be reproduced.
Somebody else, on their own machine, gets the same result. It is the difference between a finding and a story.
The program builds without complaint. That is all it means. It says nothing about whether the program is correct.
Handing the hard cases up to something bigger and more expensive, after the cheap thing has had its go.
Whatever is left after the automatic tools have taken everything they can. By definition, the awkward part.
A line in the record saying where this particular file came from and under whose rules. No entry, not finished.
Made up on purpose, as an exercise. Flagged here wherever it appears, so it is never mistaken for a finding.
Something the work cannot do, written down by the person who made it. Published here rather than buried.
Other experts going over the work before anyone trusts it. Slow, awkward, and the reason published science is worth more than a blog post.
An operating system built to try an idea, not to be relied on. Interesting to read, not something to put your bank on.
Safe to rely on for real work, where it matters if it breaks. A very high bar, and claimed far more often than it is met.
An early version handed to volunteers to find what breaks, before anyone is asked to depend on it.
Agreeing exactly what is and is not included, before starting. It is what stops a small job quietly becoming a large one.
Building up from what you know is true, instead of copying what everyone else does and hoping they were right.
Shown to be true by argument, not by testing it a lot and finding no problem. A proof covers every case at once.
A picture where colour means how much. Red for busy, blue for quiet.
A best guess, labelled as a guess. It is there so you can argue with it, not so you can rely on it.
A suggestion worth looking into. Not evidence, and not an accusation.
Two different things. On this site: software that follows where things are. On the web: hidden code that reports what you did to somebody else.
A small note a website leaves in your browser to recognise you later. This site leaves none.
Working out, from lots of separate sightings, which ones are the same thing. A camera sees a dot; tracking says which dot is which person.
The software's idea of one thing it is following: where it is, how fast, and how sure it is. Not the thing itself, only the belief about it.
One moment when a sensor noticed something. It says where, roughly, and nothing about what it was.
Carrying on with a guess when nothing can see the thing any more. The guess gets worse the longer it goes on, and good software says so.
Put aside rather than thrown away. The software stops claiming it knows where something is, but keeps what it learned in case it turns up again.
Deciding that a thing that just turned up is one you had seen before, not a new one.
When software mixes two things up and gives one of them the other's name. Everything it later says about either is then wrong.
Something the software thinks is there and is not. Usually a sensor error it took seriously.
How sure the software is that a thing is there at all, kept apart from where it thinks it is. Those are two different questions.
Guessing where something is by keeping thousands of possible answers at once and letting evidence kill off the wrong ones.
Deciding which new sighting belongs to which thing already being followed. Get it wrong and two things swap names.
What is normal for one particular thing: where it goes, and when. Useful because odd behaviour only means something against a habit.
Two things about to meet. Software can often tell before either has arrived, from where they are heading.
A box on a ship or aircraft that keeps announcing where it is. Switching it off is how something disappears on purpose.
The tracking engine on this site. It works out which sightings are the same thing, and holds on to that thing while nothing can see it.
The method TRACE uses to follow several things at once. Its trick is treating whether a thing is there as a separate question from where it is.
One number for how well a tracker did. It counts misses, things that were never there, and mix-ups, all together.
Public video with every person in it marked by hand, so anyone's tracker can be tested on the same footage.
When one thing passes behind another and cannot be seen. Brief, ordinary, and the main reason a tracker loses things.
A short summary of what something looks like, kept so it can be told apart from something else nearby.
How a thing moves — how fast and which way — without asking what is pushing it.
A name you meet on things that either happen or do not, with a number for how likely. Here: whether a track is real at all.
Finding a good whole answer by fixing one piece at a time, over and over, until the whole thing settles down.
Something that changes step by step, where what happens next depends only on where it is now, not on how it got there.
A way of describing something that wanders about but keeps being pulled back. A boat on a mooring, not a boat adrift.
Several bell curves added together, to describe a thing that one bell curve cannot. Used here to learn where an entity usually goes.
How good the evidence is, rather than how much of it there is. Many weak reports can look like certainty; this is what notices.
How wrong a number might be. Reporting it is the difference between a measurement and a guess.
Nvidia's way of running your own code on a graphics card instead of the main processor. Good at doing the same sum thousands of times.
Instructions that let one processor do the same sum on eight numbers at once instead of one at a time.
The part of a computer that does the actual work, one instruction after another. Everything else is storage or wiring.
A chip built to do thousands of small sums at the same time. Made for drawing pictures, now used for maths of any kind.
Sizes. A byte is about one letter. A thousand of them is a KB, a million an MB, a billion a GB. A thousand GB is a TB.
The list of instructions a chip understands. Two chips with the same list can run the same program without it being rebuilt.
A small fast note of where things were last found in memory, so the computer does not have to look them up again.
A chip you rewire rather than program. Slower than a purpose-built one, but you can change your mind.
A language for describing a chip rather than a program. You write what the wiring does, and a tool works out the wiring.
The tiny program that runs first when you press the power button, before anything else exists.
Translating a program into machine instructions while it is already running, rather than beforehand. Slower to start, faster after.
A pretend computer that real computers imitate, so one program can run anywhere without being rebuilt for each machine.
A program drawn as a tree rather than as text, which is the shape every tool that reads code actually works on.
A family of chip designs. Phones, and now laptops and servers. The other family is the one in most desktops.
Programs that turn source code into something a machine can run. Different ones, same job, and they disagree in the corners.
Plain-text ways of writing data down so two programs can pass it between them. Readable by a person, at a pinch.
The part you see and touch. Everything underneath is arranged to serve it, or ought to be.
The rules computers follow to pass messages over a network, and to notice when one goes missing.
A way of turning any file into one short number. Change a single letter and the number changes completely.
An old and widely used way of locking a message with one key so that only the other key opens it.
A file that looks the same everywhere, because it carries its own layout rather than trusting the reader's.
A common way for one program to ask another for something over the network, using ordinary web requests.
A way of storing files that checks its own work, so a disk quietly corrupting a file is noticed rather than passed on.
A family of free-software licences, and the project that wrote them. Sharing is the condition of use, not a nice extra.
About the most permissive licence there is: do what you like, keep the notice, expect no promises.
Ready-made licences for writing, pictures and data, in a few strengths from “credit me” upward.
A public body that publishes the reference version of things, so everyone can mean the same thing by them.
How the rules of the internet are written down and agreed. The name means Request For Comments, and that was not a joke.
A way of running Linux programs inside Windows without a second machine.
One of the two main desktops for Linux: the windows, the panel, the settings. The other is GNOME.
Ways of splitting one job across many processors or many machines, and getting the pieces back in order.
A guard that checks a program only jumps where it was built to jump, so an attacker cannot redirect it mid-run.
A design with a fixed set of states and rules for moving between them. Easy to check, because you can list every case.
The bridge between numbers and voltages. One turns a number into a signal; the other turns a signal into a number.
Everything a country produces in a year, added up and priced. A rough number that gets treated as a precise one.
A body that lends money to countries in trouble, and attaches conditions. Its figures are widely used as a reference.
Dollars. Named here because the same number means different things in different currencies, and this site says which.
What it costs to make each unit, before rent, wages or anything else. The floor under a price.
What a thing costs over its whole life, not just to buy: running it, fixing it, and getting rid of it.
One specific item as a shop lists it. Two sizes of the same thing are two of these.
An agreement not to repeat what you are about to be told. Normal in business, and a reason some work cannot be shown.
The American body that decides whether a drug or device may be sold there. Approval is slow on purpose.
An American exchange, and the source of the volatility index that gets quoted as a measure of market fear.
Software for maps that carry data — not a picture of a place, but a place you can ask questions of.
Information that came from a person talking to another person, rather than from a sensor or a computer.
The square of black and white blocks a phone camera reads. It is just a short piece of text, stored oddly.
Light just past the blue end of what an eye can see. It carries enough energy to break things and to set glues.
The body that runs world chess and hands out the ratings. A rating is a number for how strong a player is.
The gap between two percentages. Going from 40% to 45% is five of these, not a five per cent rise.
The set of ready-made lists, maps and sorting that comes with C++. Using it is the default; writing your own is the exception.
WebAssembly written out as readable text instead of bytes, so a person can look at what a browser is about to run.
The part of LLVM that assembles machine code while a program is already running, and hands it back ready to call.
The halfway language a graphics card program is shipped in. The driver turns it into real instructions for whichever card is present.
A single-file format for a trained model, holding the weights and everything needed to run them. Made for running one on your own machine.
Two headers a web server can send to wall a page off from other pages. Some browser features are only allowed behind them.
How Linux decided for years which program runs next: give everyone a fair share of time, and track who is owed.
Two of the handful of slots a processor keeps for itself. One remembers where it is; the other remembers where it came from.
Improving something by making a small random change, keeping it if it helped, and throwing it away if it did not.
A rule of thumb for chess engines: look first at taking a big piece with a small one. It is usually the best move and cheap to spot.
A way of building a pretend network where new arrivals prefer to attach to whoever is already popular. It produces a few huge hubs.
A bell curve with fatter edges, for when rare big surprises happen more often than a plain bell curve would allow.
A family of methods for stepping an equation forward in time that stay stable when the thing being solved changes very fast.
Squeezing hot metal from every side at once until the last pores close. It turns a pressed powder into a solid part.
Usually machine learning: getting a program to work something out from examples rather than from rules. On the language page it is an old family of languages instead.
A stack of three tracking tricks used together. It is built for targets whose motion now and then jumps far more than a bell curve would allow.
Working out what comes next from what just came, and nothing else. A rough but cheap way to carry motion forward.
One of the many small blocks a graphics card is built from. Work that fits inside one avoids the slow trip to the card's main memory.
How many times a second a memory bus hands over data, in millions. Higher is faster, and it is not the same as the clock speed.
A logic gate that is on only when every input is off. It and its partner NAND can each be wired up to build any other gate.
Nudging a set of weights towards a better answer after every single example. How far it nudges depends on how wrong it just was.
How much oxygen a body can use at full effort. The standard number for stamina, and one of the hardest to move.
The ordinary way silicon chips are made. Almost everything in a phone or a laptop is built this way, which is why it is cheap.
Something whose electrical resistance changes sharply in a magnetic field. Reading a hard disk works this way. Here it is one of the odd components being modelled.
Growing a crystal out of hot gas instead of digging it up. It is how laboratory diamond is made, layer by layer, and it is already an industry.
Building a very thin, very hard coating onto a tool inside a vacuum chamber. The coating here is five such layers, each doing a different job.
The slippery outer skin of the coated tool. Almost as hard as diamond and much less sticky, so the metal slides off instead of welding itself on.
How hard a piece of steel is, on the Rockwell scale. Around 55 is hardened tool steel; 70 is about as hard as steel gets.
The cutting material people reach for when carbide gives up. It works on very hard steel, but it only comes in a few shapes, which is the gap this aims at.
Ordinary welding: melt the edges of two pieces with an electric arc and let them set. It is the everyday method the new joining process is measured against.
The other everyday way of welding. TIG and MIG together are the ordinary shop welding that the new low-temperature joining process is being compared against.
One of the standard heavy rifle rounds. It is here as a known reference point, so the numbers the simulator produces can be checked against something real.
A tough plastic — the stuff big pipes and milk bottles are made of. Chosen for the mine version here because fuel and oil do not attack it.
An additive stirred into plastic so sunlight cannot make it go brittle. It is in the recipe here because the panels sit outside in Brisbane sun.
A plastic that dissolves harmlessly inside the body. Change the recipe and it takes months rather than weeks to go, which sets how long one dose lasts.
The slower-dissolving relative of the same plastic. The very long implants use it, because it can take a year or more to disappear.
The worldwide rulebook drug regulators work from. The part named here is the one about designing quality into a medicine rather than testing for it at the end.
A virus emptied out and used as a delivery van. The thing viruses are good at — getting inside cells — is borrowed, and the harmful part is left behind.
One particular version of that delivery virus. It is the one in the mouse study cited here, which added about a fifth to male-mouse lifespan.
A tool for finding one exact spot in a cell's instructions and changing it. Cheap and precise enough that the hard part is now deciding what to change.
A molecule every cell needs to get energy out of food. It runs down with age, and topping it back up is one of the levers this work pulls.
The gene for the enzyme that rebuilds the caps on the ends of chromosomes. Switching it on is a long-life idea and a cancer risk in the same breath.
A protein carried in the blood that falls off with age. Putting it back is a much-argued-over anti-ageing idea, and one of the modules listed here.
The blood marker doctors watch when the immune system starts attacking the patient instead of the illness. Cross the line and this plan says stop.
The gene behind the insulation around nerve fibres. Too much of it and the insulation grows where it should not, which is the failure named here.
One of the pair of proteins the immune system uses to cut up and reshuffle its own genes. That is how it makes an answer to a germ it has never met.
The other half of that pair. The two work together, and this project copies what they do rather than the chemistry they do it with.
The doorway HIV uses to get into a cell. A few people are born without it, and the handful of documented cures rest on exactly that.
The software trade that designs chips and circuit boards. An export layer means the results can be opened in the tools the industry actually uses.
A version of the chip-describing language that can also say what the voltages and currents do, not just the ones and zeros.
The circuit simulator everybody uses. You describe the parts and the wires, and it works out the voltages before anything is built.
How much of the power is bouncing back instead of going out of the aerial. Too much and the amplifier cooks itself, so the design trips out.
One of the numbers that says how clean a signal source really is: how far down the loudest unwanted tone sits. This design does not state it.
How loud something is, written as a number. Here it is the bang of a gun going off, and how much of it hearing protection takes away.
The switch in the emergency circuit. It slams the power to earth the moment something goes wrong, which is cruder and much faster than asking nicely.
The nuclear battery that already exists: heat from decaying material turned straight into electricity. Its 6.6% is what the proposal here is measured against.
The British nuclear research body. With Bristol it made the 2024 carbon-14 diamond cell — the one real device everything else here is stretched out from.
A flaw in diamond: one carbon atom missing, with a nitrogen atom next to it. The flaw behaves like a tiny sensor you can read with light.
The treaty under which most countries promise not to build nuclear weapons. The ten-warhead idea on this page would break Australia's promise, and it says so.
How much of the bottle is actually alcohol, as a percentage. Most spirits sit near forty; sixty here is strong on purpose, to pull flavour out of what soaks in it.
A hardness reading: press a diamond point into the surface with a set load and measure the dent. Bigger number, harder surface.
The joint Australian and New Zealand standards. Certifying a product against them is what lets you sell it here, and it is neither quick nor cheap.
The body that says a testing lab can be trusted. Getting certified needs results from a lab it has approved, which costs both money and time.
The emergency service that would actually buy a flood barrier. How slowly it buys things is listed here as an unsolved commercial problem, not a solved one.
Working out whether a part will bend or buckle by cutting it into small pieces in a computer. Here it agreed exactly with the hand calculation.
A standard file describing how a chip's pins behave in a circuit. Somebody else can then simulate a board without being shown what is inside the chip.
A small shoulder-fired weapon, in between a pistol and a rifle. Here it shares its cartridge with the pistol, which is the point of the shared parts list.
The sensor itself. A speck of diamond small enough to inject into the blood, which reports what is around it by how it glows.
A tiny circuit that turns a handful of stored bits into a long run of random-looking ones. Cheap and repeatable, and not a secret on its own.
A running average that quietly forgets the past, so it follows what is happening now instead of being held back by last month.
A detector that adds up how far readings drift from normal and speaks when the total gets too big. It catches a small steady shift one reading would hide.
Holding something steady by watching how far off it is, how long it has been off, and how fast it is moving. A thermostat works this way.
Radio frequency: signals that wiggle fast enough to be broadcast rather than heard. Everything from a radio station to a phone to a radar lives up there.
The power amplifier: the last stage, which takes a small signal and makes it big enough to actually go out. It is what turns this design into a hazard.
The hard grain a carbide cutting tool is made of. On its own it is brittle, so it is bonded together with a softer metal — the Co in WC-Co.
The oldest light there is, left over from when the universe first went clear. It is the furthest thing anyone can see, which is why it turns up here.
Einstein's theory of gravity: heavy things bend space and time, and everything else follows the bend. The dispute on this page is between two readings of it.
The standard model of an expanding universe, named after the four people who wrote it down. The essay defends it rather than attacking it.
The research group whose published mouse result is cited here: a gene therapy that added about a fifth to male-mouse lifespan. Cited as real, not claimed.
The poisoned-air end of the threat list — chemical, biological and radiation weapons — and the masks and filters meant to keep them out.
An agreed table of how thick the air is at each height. Two people working out a bullet's flight then start from the same air, so the answers can be compared.
The armour rating everyone quotes. The two points the model is anchored to are one that stops a pistol round and one that stops a rifle round.
The standard explosive, and the one everything else gets compared against. Here it is a mixture being described on paper, not a thing being built.
One of the old text-prediction methods, from before neural networks. It guesses the next letter from the last few, which is the ceiling this work aims to break.
The current generation of computer memory sticks. Each generation moves more data per second than the last, and this is the fifth of them.
Rules that stop many processor cores disagreeing about what is in memory. Each letter is one state a cached copy is allowed to be in.
Shared data handled the way a bank handles a transfer: a block of changes either all happens or none of it does. Nothing is ever left half done.
A way of quoting how much raw work a chip gets through each second. Easy to print on a slide; the audit here could not check it without the hardware.
How a graphics chip runs many threads at once: a group of them must all take the same branch. When they disagree it runs both, wasting half the work.
A brand of consumer graphics card. The 3090 is one of them, and the audit did not have one, so those speed figures stayed unchecked.
A random answer that comes with a proof it was not rigged. Anyone can check the proof, and nobody gets to choose the answer.
Deciding whose turn it is to talk when many devices share one channel. Collision-free means no two of them ever end up talking over each other.
A part that behaves the same way every time and simply adds up: double the input, double the output. Most of the easy maths assumes this. These devices do not.
A modest promise about a controller: keep the demands on it within bounds and its response stays within bounds too. It will not run away.
How long a detector runs before it cries wolf when nothing is actually wrong. Here it is about 3,500 steps between false alarms.
Small enough to go in through a vein, on a drip, rather than needing surgery. On this page that is an assumption, not something anyone has shown.
Steady current that does not wiggle at all. At the bottom of a frequency range it means zero, so the band starts from nothing and goes up.
The paper's own name for the single idea underneath its three results. Keep nudging a guess along a little at a time, on a curved space rather than a flat one.
The program on this site that hides who is talking to whom. Encryption hides what you said; this hides that you spoke at all.
Two things on this site. The encryption scheme that works out its own one-time number instead of sending it. And ARIA-INTEL, the tracking prototype behind SENTINEL.
The crime-analysis program on this site. It reads public crime data and ranks where to look next. Every lead traces back to the record it came from.
The short name for ParanoidBSD, the operating system built here. It moves a hardened BSD system to C++23 and gives each program only the access it needs.
The short name for HardenedBSD on these pages. ParanoidBSD keeps its hardening and builds the new security model on top of it.
Two different things here. In the compression work: a way of scoring a trained network by how hard it squeezes data. In the drug work: a solvent that sets a gel once it meets water.
One of three compression frameworks here. It puts perfect and lossy squeezing on one sliding scale instead of treating them as two separate kinds of thing.
Energy-Resource Economic Model. It measures what a country is worth in units of energy instead of money, so the figure does not rest on trusting a bank.
Total National Wealth. The single number in that energy model: a country's energy, factories, food, water and people, all added up in one physical unit.
The main American share index. The paper counts how many bets are placed on it, 867 times more than in 1999, and asks where that ends.
A whole invented country, worked out on paper: government, money, defence, drugs, foreign policy. The point is that the parts must not contradict each other.
General Purpose Networks. One of the invented AI families in the fictional-country folder, written up with real theorem statements although the systems do not exist.
Torpedo Data Computer. The US Navy's 1932 aiming machine for submarines, rebuilt here as software and measured, including the drag and momentum of its own gears.
A design where the optimiser, the scheduler and the memory turn out to be one trick. One piece of machinery, doing every job.
Universal Statistical Generator. A text generator that counts patterns instead of training a network, using a fixed-size table so long context stops costing so much.
Unified Hash-Predictive Memory. It looks things up and works things out with one set of sums, rather than bolting memory onto a model afterwards.
Verification-Enabled Reasoning and Integrated Theorem-Acquiring System. It checks that each learning step is allowed before taking it, rather than proving afterwards that it was.
A way of recognising things, copied from the immune system. The body builds defences against germs it has never met by mixing a small set of parts.
Logarithmic Complexity Reduction Principle. The claim that the many places where a slow method becomes a fast one are all the same few tricks, not separate luck.
Quantum Graph Optimisation. A pipeline that pretends to be a quantum computer on an ordinary one, and treats the noise as useful information rather than a nuisance.
The gravity theory on the physics shelf. It lets gravity reach across distance in a new way while still never sending a signal faster than light.
A way of joining two pieces of metal without melting them. Heat, electricity and sound work together in a chemical bath, instead of a costly vacuum chamber.
The prefix naming the five settings of that metal-joining process. ULTRA-FLASH is two minutes at 150 °C; ULTRA-PRECISION takes half an hour or more, hotter.
The cutting-tool design on the shelf: a carbide tip that changes composition through its thickness, aimed at hard metals where ordinary tools give out.
A thought experiment about building a quantum computer out of flaws in diamond that work at room temperature. Most of the paper is the seven reasons it cannot be done yet.
Neural Quantum Dust. Tiny diamond specks injected into the blood to listen to single brain cells, read by dust-sized chips powered by ultrasound from outside.
A written-out plan for changing human genes to raise what a body can do. It is labelled speculation, and it publishes its own guess at the harm: 20 to 32 percent.
Three of the four genes that can wind a grown cell back towards a younger state. The fourth is left out on purpose.
A real published trial of the drug rapamycin. The human-enhancement paper cites it as a genuine result, to separate what is real from what it is only imagining.
An invented drug in the medicines folder, written up with a full made-up file. Every invented compound there carries a banner saying it is fiction.
The body-armour system in the police and defence folders. The police version is specified at 6.5 kg against the 20.25 kg gear it would replace.
One of four random-number generators on the shelf. It uses old, well-understood arithmetic at a very large size, and is the one put through the standard test battery.
Quality control. Checking the work as it is being done, rather than finding out at the end that a whole batch is wrong.
Central bank digital currency: money issued by a country's central bank in electronic form, rather than as notes and coins. Many countries are now working on one.
Cold dark matter, the standard picture of what the universe is mostly made of. ΛCDM is that picture plus the force pushing the universe apart.
A proposed change to the rule limiting how precisely you can pin down a particle. The paper notes it could clash with very fine measurements unless the effect is tiny.
The usual way a group of computers agrees on something when some of them may lie or fail. It works, but everybody has to message everybody.
Several parties working out an answer together without any of them revealing what they put in. Each learns the result and nothing else.
A function that turns any input into output nobody can tell from random, unless they hold the key. Much of modern encryption is built on one.
Using a cipher by numbering the blocks and scrambling the numbers, so you can jump straight to any part without working through the rest.
The common way of using AES so it both scrambles a message and catches tampering. It needs a number used once, and breaks badly if that number repeats.
Information-set decoding, the best known way of attacking codes like the one this scheme leans on. Its cost is what the security claim is measured against.
The property that nobody can forge a new valid message tag. The page says this scheme has no proof of it yet, which is the honest thing to say.
The fair test for a forging attack. The attacker is first allowed to ask for tags on any messages they like, then has to forge a new one.
Writing a yes-or-no rule as nothing but ANDs and exclusive-ORs. Every such rule has exactly one form like this, which makes two of them easy to compare.
Short for a finite field: arithmetic with only a fixed, finite set of numbers, where results wrap around instead of running off. GF(2) has just 0 and 1.
A set of points joined by one-way arrows, with no way to follow the arrows in a circle. Useful whenever one thing must happen before another.
One of the oldest ways of making random-looking numbers: multiply, add, keep the remainder, repeat. Fast and simple, and not random enough on its own.
A random number generator. A machine or piece of code that produces numbers with no pattern anyone can find, which much of security rests on.
A recipe for solving hard choosing problems on a quantum computer. Here it is only simulated on an ordinary machine, and no advantage is claimed.
A fast way of breaking a signal into the simple waves that make it up. It is one of the most used pieces of maths in computing.
The library most people reach for when they need that wave-splitting done fast. Named here as the kind of tuned code these results were not compared against.
Exploring a network by taking every step one hop from where you are before going any deeper. It finds the shortest route first.
Exploring a network by following one path as far as it goes, then backing up and trying the next. Uses far less memory than the alternative.
The standard way of guessing where something is from noisy readings. It keeps one running best guess and nudges it as each new reading arrives.
Several different guesses about how a thing is moving, all running at once. The evidence decides which one to believe right now.
Deciding which sighting belongs to which tracked thing. It weighs every possible pairing at once rather than committing to one and being wrong.
The score used to mark a tracker's work. It rolls missed things, invented things and how far off the positions were into one number you can compare.
The part of the tracker that measures its own noise while it runs. How jumpy the sensor is, and how jumpy the movement is, instead of being told up front.
A check on whether a run of numbers still resembles itself a few steps later. If it does when it should not, something has gone wrong.
The usual way of saying how far off a set of guesses was, on average. Big misses count for more than small ones, on purpose.
A single number saying which of two answers the evidence favours, and by how much. Positive one way, negative the other, zero for no idea.
A running average that quietly forgets the past: each new number counts a little, and everything older fades. Cheap, and it never has to store the history.
A way of measuring how alike two things are that only cares how far apart they sit. Similar things score high, distant things score near zero.
A way of hashing that puts similar things in the same bucket on purpose. It is how you find the nearest match without comparing against everything.
A model of something that moves through hidden states you cannot see directly, where each state leaves clues. Speech and handwriting were done this way for years.
Short for neural network. Layers of simple sums stacked up, where the stack as a whole does something useful and no single layer does much.
The plainest kind of neural network: layers where every unit feeds every unit in the next layer, and nothing loops back.
A kind of neural network with a memory it can choose to keep or wipe, built for sequences. It was the standard before attention took over.
Two networks trained against each other: one makes fakes, the other tries to spot them. Both get better until the fakes are hard to tell apart.
A version of that two-network setup with a different scoring rule, meant to stop training collapsing. It was tried here against AES, and still failed.
The usual score for a yes-or-no answer. It punishes a model harder the more confident it was when it got the answer wrong.
One of the small bending functions placed between layers of a network. Without one, a stack of layers would collapse into a single straight-line sum.
How most models are trained: look at a small batch, nudge the settings a little in the direction that helps, repeat millions of times.
Training something that reads a sequence by unrolling it into one long chain. The blame for the final answer is then traced back through every step.
A plan for how fast a model learns during training. Warm up, hold steady for most of the run, then slow down at the end.
Data that looks nothing like anything the model was trained on. Its answers there stop meaning much, and it will usually not admit that.
A tidier version of the random-features trick, where the random directions are spread out evenly rather than drawn at random. Building it here found a real bug.
A way of promising a learner will probably be roughly right. It says how many examples you need before the odds of being badly wrong are small.
Algorithmic learning theory. It counts how many mistakes a learner can make before it settles down, rather than how much data it needs.
Getting software to handle written language. On this site it means the old rule-based kind, chosen because a police tool has to be able to explain itself.
